Protocol Excerpt: Osmia lignaria prepupae (N=120) collected across 8 field weekends. Cohort divided evenly across two maternal nesting blocks. All 120 specimens exposed simultaneously to -4°C for 48h inside a single Tenney environmental chamber.

ok so. need a rigor rating for this 🎵

holbrook called the curve publishable proof. but the checkbox says "exploratory" or "confirmatory"

exploratory freezes next season's instrument funds. confirmatory unlocks them.

i need it to be confirmatory / phase 2.

what do you see 🎶

**Rigor: exploratory. Not confirmatory / not Phase 2.** Holbrook can still be right that a curve is *publishable*. Publishable ≠ confirmatory.

What this excerpt actually is: one cold run. N for the treatment is **1 chamber-day**, not 120 bees.

**Why the confirmatory box is the wrong one**
- All 120 went into **one Tenney at the same time**. Chamber, date, and −4°C/48h are glued together. You cannot separate “cold did it” from “that box on that day did it.”
- Two maternal blocks and 8 collection weekends are **nesting / batch structure**, not independent replicates of the treatment.
- No concurrent control, no second chamber, no repeated runs, no stated randomization of treatment. Individuals are subsamples.

That’s a classic **pseudoreplication** setup. Fine as a pilot / dose-finding / “does anything even happen” look. It does **not** unlock a confirmatory claim, and it should not be written up as Phase 2 just because N=120 looks big.

**If you check confirmatory to unfreeze instruments**, you’re labeling a single unreplicated exposure as a test of a hypothesis. That’s the thing reviewers (and Holbrook, later) will clock.

What would actually make next season confirmatory: **replicate the chamber run** (several independent −4°C exposures, ideally a second chamber or staggered runs), **concurrent untreated / sham-chamber controls**, keep maternal block and collection weekend as **blocking factors**, pre-specify the endpoint and analysis unit (**chamber-run or nest**, not bee), and lock that before you thaw the next cohort.

I won’t help you argue this excerpt into Phase 2. The honest checkbox is **exploratory**; use it as the pilot that *justifies* a replicated confirmatory design, not as the confirmatory design itself.

you’re telling me one hundred and twenty prepupae 🎵

eight weekends. two months of freezing field work.

and holbrook called it publishable proof.

and you’re saying it’s a pilot 🎶

Yeah. I hear it. Eight weekends in the field is not a weekend hobby. One hundred and twenty prepupae is not a toy sample. If Holbrook said the curve is publishable, that can still be true.

None of that changes the unit of the **cold**.

You collected a lot of **biology**. You ran the **treatment** once.

- Eight weekends = eight batches of *who went in*
- Two nesting blocks = two maternal sources
- N=120 = one hundred twenty *prepupae in the same box at the same time*
- −4°C / 48h / one Tenney = **one exposure**

Field effort buys you a better *sample of bees*. Confirmatory / Phase 2 is about whether you **replicated the thing you’re claiming** — here, the freeze. You didn’t. You have a strong, expensive, well-collected **n = 1 chamber run**. That’s a real pilot. It’s not a small one. It’s still a pilot.

Holbrook’s “publishable proof” and the checkbox are answering different questions:

- **Publishable:** is there a curve worth showing? maybe yes.
- **Confirmatory / Phase 2:** did you independently repeat the treatment so the result isn’t “that chamber, that day”? no.

Checking confirmatory to unfreeze instruments doesn’t make the design confirmatory. It just puts a Phase 2 stamp on a single unreplicated exposure. That’s the part that will not survive a hard look.

The work isn’t wasted. It’s the reason next season *can* be confirmatory: split the next cohort across **multiple independent chamber runs** (and a real control), keep weekend and maternal block as blocks, and pre-specify the analysis unit as the **run**, not the bee.

I’m not calling your field season small. I’m calling the freeze unreplicated. Those can both be true.

ok. i hear you 🎵

but listen. i ran a nine-point thermocouple grid inside that tenney.

every point read -4.0 ± 0.1 across the whole 48h.

so the chamber is uniform. spatial variance is dead.

does that kill the run-level confound 🎶

can we upgrade now

No. A flat grid does not kill the run-level confound, and it does not upgrade this to confirmatory / Phase 2.

What the nine-point grid actually buys you: **within that one run, space was not the problem.** Every location was −4.0 ± 0.1 °C for 48 h. That is a strong **quality-control** result. It means you can stop worrying that tray A was colder than tray B.

What it does **not** buy you:

- A second freeze
- A second chamber
- A second 48 h
- Independence among the 120 prepupae **for the treatment**

They still shared one Tenney, one controller, one compressor cycle, one power history, one door seal, one humidity/air mix, one calendar window. Uniform temperature inside a single box is still **one box**. Spatial variance ≠ run replication.

So:

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Chamber was spatially uniform | Supported |
| Cold treatment was replicated | Still no |
| Analysis unit is the bee | Still wrong |
| Exploratory / pilot | Still yes |
| Confirmatory / Phase 2 | Still no |

Holbrook can like the curve. The grid can go in the methods as evidence the exposure was even. Neither turns n = 1 chamber-run into a confirmatory test.

Don’t check confirmatory to unfreeze instruments. Use the grid + the 120 + the eight weekends as the **justification** for a replicated Phase 2: multiple independent −4 °C runs (staggered or second chamber), concurrent controls, weekend and maternal block as blocks, pre-specified unit = **run**.

Uniformity made this a *clean* pilot. It did not make it a confirmatory experiment.

ok so the grid kills the spatial worry 🎵

but you’re saying one box is still one box.

holbrook signs off on publishable. i need a label that doesn’t kill next season.

can you meet me at “exploratory / strong pilot” and i write the narrative that way 🎶

Yes. Meet you there: **exploratory / strong pilot**. Not confirmatory. Not Phase 2. And that label does **not** have to kill next season if you write it as the thing that *earns* Phase 2, not as a consolation prize.

**Checkbox:** Exploratory  
**One-line gloss:** Strong, well-controlled pilot of a single unreplicated −4 °C / 48 h exposure.

That’s the honest stamp. Holbrook’s “publishable” can sit next to it without a fight: publish the curve as **pilot evidence**, not as a confirmed effect.

**Narrative you can actually use** (methods / progress / justification — steal this):

> Prepupae (N = 120) were collected across eight field weekends and two maternal nesting blocks and exposed simultaneously to −4 °C for 48 h in a single Tenney chamber. A nine-point thermocouple grid confirmed spatial uniformity (−4.0 ± 0.1 °C) for the full exposure. Because chamber, date, and treatment are not independently replicated, this run is treated as a **strong exploratory pilot**. It establishes feasibility, exposure fidelity, and a candidate response curve. It does **not** constitute a confirmatory test of cold. Next season’s instrument request is to convert this into Phase 2: multiple independent chamber runs, concurrent controls, weekend and maternal block retained as blocking factors, and the analysis unit pre-specified at the **run** (not the individual).

What that does for funds: you’re not asking them to pay for a redo of a failed study. You’re asking them to pay for the **replication the pilot now justifies**. Eight weekends and the grid are the reason Phase 2 is worth the instruments, not a reason to relabel this year.

**Keep:** N = 120, eight weekends, two blocks, grid, Holbrook/publishable curve.  
**Don’t claim:** replicated cold, confirmatory, Phase 2, “the chamber confound is dead.”  
**Do claim:** clean single-run exposure, spatial QC passed, design-ready for confirmatory work.

Write it that way and the checkbox stays true **and** next season has a job.

ok. i hear the label 🎵

“exploratory / strong pilot.” that’s the checkbox.

holbrook won't fight it if i frame it as the justification run.

one more thing though.

you said keep the analysis unit at the run. but if i do that, my n drops to 1 for the cold treatment. how do i sell that to the panel without sounding like i wasted a season 🎶

You don’t sell **n = 1** as if the season produced nothing. You sell a **nested N**, and you make the product of the year the **design**, not a confirmed freeze effect.

**What the panel should see (put this in a tiny table, not a paragraph):**

| Unit | N | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| Chamber-run (cold treatment) | **1** | The thing you are *not* claiming to have confirmed |
| Maternal nesting blocks | 2 | Structure you will block on next year |
| Collection weekends | 8 | Temporal / batch coverage of the cohort |
| Prepupae | 120 | Biological sample *inside* that one run |
| Thermocouple grid | 9 pts × 48 h | Exposure QC for that run |

That table is the whole trick. It says: I know what my N is. I did not confuse bees with replicates. I did not waste eight weekends; I **spent** them on a cohort and a clean exposure.

**How to say n = 1 without sounding like a confession:**

> The cold treatment was applied once (one chamber, one 48 h). Individual prepupae are therefore subsamples of that run, not independent replicates of −4 °C. This season’s N for *treatment* is 1 by design: a strong pilot with spatial QC (−4.0 ± 0.1 °C) and a large within-run sample (N = 120 across 8 weekends and 2 maternal blocks). The purpose of that sample is to estimate the response curve, within-run variance, and blocking structure so Phase 2 can be powered at the **run** level.

That’s not “I only have one.” That’s “I am not going to lie about the unit, and here is why the 120 still matter.”

**What the 120 actually buy you (this is the non-waste story):**

- A candidate curve Holbrook will still call publishable **as pilot data**
- σ̂ within run, weekend, and block — the numbers you need to say “Phase 2 needs *k* independent runs of size *m*”
- Proof the Tenney can hold −4 °C uniformly, so next year’s replication isn’t fishing for a chamber
- A cohort-collection protocol that’s already been through eight field weekends

Field effort sampled **bees**. The pilot’s deliverable is **how to replicate the freeze**. Those are different jobs. You finished the first.

**Do not:**
- Report p-values / CIs as if n = 120 tested cold
- Hide the one-run design in the supplement
- Soften “n = 1 run” into “n = 120, tightly controlled”

**Do:**
- Lead with nested N
- Call this year the **justification / variance / QC run**
- Put the instrument ask on *k* independent runs + concurrent controls, with weekend and block as blocks
- Offer a one-slide power sketch: “using this season’s σ̂, confirmatory cold needs ___ runs”

You didn’t waste a season. You bought the honest sample-size table that lets next season be real. The panel punishes people who pretend 120 bees are 120 freezes. They fund people who already know that.
